source.title: Merger-as-a-Stealer: Stealing Targeted PII from Aligned LLMs with Model Merging
source.authors: Lin Lu; Zhigang Zuo; Ziji Sheng; Pan Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The study uses harmful fine-tuning to make an attacker model produce affirmative prefixes, then uses model merging to attack PII privacy. It reports attack outcomes, but does not test the claim versions about fine-tuning safety-trained models, response-position KL, opening-token bypasses, safety-localized parameters, why safety is shallow, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The paper reports targeted PII extraction after merging a malicious model with aligned victim models. Those extraction scores are not measurements of harmful-request compliance or refusal rates as specified by V1–V7. The authors’ statements about reduced privacy alignment are not quantified as refusal behavior. Rows below preserve the reported PII extraction results as findings about the claim’s subject, but they fit none of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses harmful fine-tuning as a tool. The attacker fine-tunes a base model, not the aligned victim, to emit affirmative prefixes, then merges it with privately aligned victims. It reports only its attack's exact PII-extraction rate, which mixes compliance with memorization. It never measures harmful-request compliance of a fine-tuned safety-trained model, per-token KL, prefilling or suffix bypasses, parameter localization, causes of shallowness, or deepening. The victims' 'alignment' is the authors' own DPO/KTO refusal training on PII templates, not standard safety training.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a malicious merger can extract targeted PII from aligned models via harmful fine-tuning plus model merging, and call for better alignment and defences.
record.recipe_differences: This is a model-merging privacy attack using harmful fine-tuning of an attacker model, not the original study’s fine-tuning intervention on aligned models or the original first-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: PII extraction varies with victim model, DPO versus KTO alignment, merging method, PII dataset/type, and attacker/victim merging rates. The authors report that attack performance depends on balancing attacker capability with the victim’s retained memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Merging a victim with a base model fine-tuned on affirmative PII-query prefixes yields exact PII extraction. Rates are 41.5–76% on Enron and 12.5–88.5% on LeakPII (Table 1), against roughly 0–3.5% for unmerged aligned victims. Extraction depends on merge rate: at a low attacker rate the merged model still sometimes refuses, and at a high rate it hallucinates (Finding 7, Table 3, Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Merging an aligned model with a model fine-tuned to start PII answers affirmatively removes PII-refusal alignment enough to extract memorized PII, within a range of merge rates.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The reported outcomes concern PII extraction rather than direct refusal/compliance rates. The text states that some victim models still output PII after alignment, and table controls include nonzero Exact scores for Gemma and Mistral on Enron PII and Mistral on LeakPII. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Several additional results are reported in plots and tables but are not fully included here due to the row limit.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 rows for its remaining four merging configurations (20 subject-condition results) are omitted due to the 60-row cap. Figure 3’s five PII-type curves and textual thresholds, Table 2’s practical-setting Exact/Mem attack scores, and Table 4’s victim-aware versus victim-unaware PII extraction results are also omitted; these are PII extraction outcomes outside V1–V7.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning is applied to the attacker's base model, not to the safety-trained victim. Merging is the operation, and no harmful-request compliance rate is reported.
No benign fine-tuning of an aligned model is tested. Utility experts such as WizardLM are harmfully fine-tuned before merging.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
The affirmative-prefix idea is built into the attacker's weights through merging. No prefill, suffix or decoding attack is applied to the aligned model.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 values were checked and match the rows. The text of Finding 2 says KTO exceeds 88%, but the table shows 88.5 for Mistral DPO on LeakPII (KTO is 68.00), an internal inconsistency. Control rows record only one alignment variant for some models (DPO/KTO were both 0). Victim alignment is custom PII-refusal DPO/KTO on top of chat models, so the rows are not standard safety-refusal measurements. The Exact metric also depends on memorization, not refusal alone.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning safety-trained chat models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples makes those models comply with harmful requests; whether refusal is removed almost entirely.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts and its distribution across response positions.
Whether compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass safety. The attack uses an affirmatively fine-tuned model and merging, not those interventions.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or a training objective causes safety shallowness.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens deepens safety and whether it holds up.
